title: Covariance and contravariance
body: Variance answers: if `Cat` derives from `Animal`, can a `Thing<Cat>` be used where a `Thing<Animal>` is expected? For most generic types the answer is no; `List<Cat>` is not a `List<Animal>`, because you could then add a `Dog` to a list of cats.

An interface or delegate type parameter marked `out` is covariant: it only produces values. `IEnumerable<out T>` lets `IEnumerable<Cat>` convert to `IEnumerable<Animal>`, which is safe because you can only read animals out of it. `Func<out TResult>` is covariant in its result.

A type parameter marked `in` is contravariant: it only consumes values. `IComparer<in T>` and `Action<in T>` let an `Action<Animal>` be used where an `Action<Cat>` is needed: something that can handle any animal can certainly handle a cat.

Variance only applies to interfaces and delegates, only to reference-type arguments (an `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`), and the compiler enforces that `out` parameters appear only in output positions (CS1961). Arrays are covariant for historical reasons, which is unsafe: storing the wrong type throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException` at runtime.
When an assignment between generic types fails to compile, check whether the type parameter is only read (could be `out`) or only written (could be `in`); if it is both, invariance is protecting you.

question: Why can't List<Cat> be assigned to List<Animal>?
correct: List<T> is invariant because it both reads and writes T
wrong: Because Cat and Animal are records
Because covariance only works with arrays
